claim: TRPC5 channel is a nonselective cation channel that participates in diverse physiological processes.
source: TRPC5 channel is a nonselective cation channel that participates in diverse physiological processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about TRPC5 function, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: TRPC5 inhibitors show promise in the treatment of anxiety disorder, depression, and kidney disease.
source: TRPC5 inhibitors show promise in the treatment of anxiety disorder, depression, and kidney disease.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on TRPC5 inhibitors in disease models, as referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of human TRPC5 in complex with clemizole was determined to 2.7 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present the cryo-EM structures of human TRPC5 in complex with two distinct inhibitors, namely clemizole and HC-070, to the resolution of 2.7 Å.
evidence: The resolution is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 4-5.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of human TRPC5 in complex with HC-070 was determined to 2.7 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present the cryo-EM structures of human TRPC5 in complex with two distinct inhibitors, namely clemizole and HC-070, to the resolution of 2.7 Å.
evidence: The resolution is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 6-7.

claim: Clemizole binds inside the voltage sensor-like domain of each subunit.
source: The structures reveal that clemizole binds inside the voltage sensor-like domain of each subunit.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps shown in Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 5E-F.

claim: HC-070 is wedged between adjacent subunits and replaces the glycerol group of a putative diacylglycerol molecule near the extracellular side.
source: In contrast, HC-070 is wedged between adjacent subunits and replaces the glycerol group of a putative diacylglycerol molecule near the extracellular side.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 7G.

claim: Mutations in the inhibitor binding pockets altered the potency of inhibitors.
source: Moreover, we found mutations in the inhibitor binding pockets altered the potency of inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figures 2E, 3E-F, and Tables 2-3.

claim: Both clemizole and HC-070 exert inhibitory functions by stabilizing the ion channel in a nonconductive closed state.
source: These structures suggest that both clemizole and HC-070 exert the inhibitory functions by stabilizing the ion channel in a nonconductive closed state.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis showing the pore is closed (Figure 4A-B) and both inhibitors are bound.

claim: The mammalian TRPC channels are Ca2+-permeable nonselective cation channels that belong to the TRP channel superfamily.
source: The mammalian transient receptor potential canonical (TRPC) channels are Ca2+-permeable nonselective cation channels that belong to the transient receptor potential (TRP) channel superfamily (Clapham, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Clapham, 2003.

claim: TRPC channels share the closest homology to the Drosophila TRP channel among all TRP subfamilies.
source: Among all the subfamilies of TRP channels, TRPC channels share the closest homology to the Drosophila TRP channel, the first TRP channel cloned (Montell and Rubin, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Montell and Rubin, 1989.

claim: TRPC2 is a pseudogene in humans.
source: The TRPC subfamily is formed by seven channels in mammals, TRPC1-TRPC7, while TRPC2 is a pseudogene in human.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: TRPC channels can be divided into TRPC1, TRPC2, TRPC3/6/7, and TRPC4/5 subgroups based on primary amino acid sequences.
source: According to the primary amino acid sequences, TRPC channels can be divided into TRPC1, TRPC2, TRPC3/6/7, and TRPC4/5 subgroups (Montell et al., 2002).
evidence: This classification is supported by citation to Montell et al., 2002.

claim: TRPC5 is mainly expressed in the brain and to a lesser extent in the liver, kidney, testis, and pancreas.
source: Among them, TRPC5 is mainly expressed in the brain and to a lesser extent in the liver, kidney, testis, and pancreas (Philipp et al., 1998; Sossey-Alaoui et al., 1999; Uhlén et al., 2015).
evidence: This expression pattern is supported by citations to Philipp et al., 1998; Sossey-Alaoui et al., 1999; Uhlén et al., 2015.

claim: TRPC5 can form homotetrameric channels or heterotetrameric channels with TRPC4 and/or TRPC1.
source: It can form homotetrameric channels or heterotetrameric channels with TRPC4 and/or TRPC1 (Chung et al., 2007; Chung et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2007; Chung et al., 2006.

claim: TRPC5 activation leads to the depolarization of cell membrane and an increase of intracellular Ca2+ level.
source: TRPC5 activation leads to the depolarization of cell membrane and an increase of intracellular Ca2+ level ([Ca2+]i).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRPC5 function.

claim: TRPC5 is implicated in fear, anxiety, depression, and progressive kidney disease in humans.
source: TRPC5 mediates diverse physiological processes and is implicated in many disease conditions in human such as fear, anxiety, depression, and progressive kidney disease (Riccio et al., 2009; Schaldecker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Riccio et al., 2009; Schaldecker et al., 2013.

claim: TRPC5 can be activated by receptor-activated Gq/11-PLC pathway upon the dissociation of Na+/H+ exchanger regulatory factor and activation of IP3 receptors.
source: TRPC5 can be activated by receptor-activated Gq/11-PLC pathway upon the dissociation of Na+/H+ exchanger regulatory factor and activation of IP3 receptors (Kanki et al., 2001; Schaefer et al., 2000; Storch et al., 2017), or through the Gi/o pathway (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanki et al., 2001; Schaefer et al., 2000; Storch et al., 2017.

claim: TRPC5 can be activated through the Gi/o pathway.
source: TRPC5 can be activated by receptor-activated Gq/11-PLC pathway upon the dissociation of Na+/H+ exchanger regulatory factor and activation of IP3 receptors (Kanki et al., 2001; Schaefer et al., 2000; Storch et al., 2017), or through the Gi/o pathway (Jeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeon et al., 2012.

claim: TRPC5 functions as a store-operated channel by interacting with STIM1.
source: By interacting with STIM1, TRPC5 functions as a store-operated channel (Asanov et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asanov et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2004.

claim: Extracellular application of reduced thioredoxin or reducing agents enhances TRPC5 activity.
source: Extracellular application of reduced thioredoxin or reducing agents enhances TRPC5 activity (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC5 is regulated by intracellular Ca2+ in a concentration-dependent bell-shaped manner.
source: TRPC5 is also regulated by [Ca2+]i in a concentration-dependent bell-shaped manner (Blair et al., 2009; Gross et al., 2009; Ordaz et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2004), and extracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]o) at concentration higher than 5 mM robustly activates TRPC5 (Schaefer et al., 2000; Zeng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blair et al., 2009; Gross et al., 2009; Ordaz et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2004.

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ at concentration higher than 5 mM robustly activates TRPC5.
source: TRPC5 is also regulated by [Ca2+]i in a concentration-dependent bell-shaped manner (Blair et al., 2009; Gross et al., 2009; Ordaz et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2004), and extracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]o) at concentration higher than 5 mM robustly activates TRPC5 (Schaefer et al., 2000; Zeng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schaefer et al., 2000; Zeng et al., 2004.

claim: (-)-Englerin A can selectively activate TRPC4/5 and inhibit tumor growth.
source: (-)-Englerin A (EA), a natural product obtained from Phyllanthus engleri, can selectively activate TRPC4/5 and therefore inhibit tumor growth (Akbulut et al., 2015; Carson et al., 2015), suggesting activation of TRPC4/5 might be a strategy to cure certain types of cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akbulut et al., 2015; Carson et al., 2015.

claim: TRPC5 inhibitors showed promising results for the treatment of central nervous system diseases and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in animal models.
source: Moreover, TRPC5 inhibitors showed promising results for the treatment of central nervous system diseases and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in animal models (Just et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Just et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017.

claim: A TRPC4/5 inhibitor developed by Hydra and Boehringer Ingelheim is currently in clinical trial for the treatment of anxiety disorder and depression.
source: A TRPC4/5 inhibitor developed by Hydra and Boehringer Ingelheim is currently in clinical trial for the treatment of anxiety disorder and depression (Wulff et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wulff et al., 2019.

claim: TRPC5 inhibitor GFB-887 developed by Goldfinch Bio is in phase 1 clinical trial for the treatment of kidney disease.
source: Another TRPC5 inhibitor GFB-887 developed by Goldfinch Bio is in phase 1 clinical trial for the treatment of kidney disease (NCT number: NCT03970122).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a clinical trial number.

claim: Clemizole is a benzimidazole-derived H1 antagonist that can inhibit TRPC5.
source: CMZ is a benzimidazole-derived H1 antagonist that can inhibit TRPC5.
evidence: This is established knowledge about clemizole.

claim: M084 and AC1903 are TRPC5 inhibitors that belong to the clemizole class.
source: M084 and AC1903 are also TRPC5 inhibitors that belong to the CMZ class (Richter et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Richter et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: HC-070 is a methylxanthine derivative that inhibits TRPC4/5 with high potency.
source: In contrast, HC-070 is a methylxanthine derivative that inhibits TRPC4/5 with high potency (Just et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Just et al., 2018.

claim: TRPC5 inhibitor Pico145 (HC-608) and activator AM237 belong to the HC-070 class.
source: TRPC5 inhibitor Pico145 (HC-608) and activator AM237 belong to this class (Just et al., 2018; Minard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Just et al., 2018; Minard et al., 2019.

claim: Extracellular calcium and EA can robustly elevate intracellular calcium concentration through hTRPC5 channel activation.
source: We show that extracellular calcium and EA can robustly elevate intracellular calcium concentration through hTRPC5 channel activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), as reported previously (Just et al., 2018; Schaefer et al., 2000; Zeng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C and citations to Just et al., 2018; Schaefer et al., 2000; Zeng et al., 2004.

claim: CMZ and HC-070 effectively inhibited the extracellular calcium-induced intracellular calcium increase in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, CMZ and HC-070 effectively inhibited the extracellular calcium-induced intracellular calcium increase in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the dose-response curves in Figure 1A-B.

claim: C-terminal truncation of mTRPC increased expression level and retained its pharmacology profile.
source: It is previously reported that the C-terminal truncation of mTRPC increased expression level and retained its pharmacology profile (Duan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duan et al., 2019.

claim: The C-terminal truncation construct hTRPC51-764 can be activated by EA and extracellular calcium and can be inhibited by HC-070 and CMZ.
source: Similarly, we found the C-terminal truncation of hTRPC5 yielded a construct (hTRPC51-764) that can be activated by EA and extracellular calcium and can be inhibited by HC-070 and CMZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The hTRPC51-764 construct showed a higher expression level of the tetrameric channel compared to full-length wild-type hTRPC5.
source: This construct showed a higher expression level of the tetrameric channel in comparison with the full-length wild-type (WT) hTRPC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by FSEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The apo state hTRPC5 structure was obtained at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: For the cryo-EM sample in the presence of EA, we obtained a reconstruction at the resolution of 3.0 Å (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: EA was not bound to the protein in the apo structure, probably due to reduced affinity of EA toward purified TRPC5 protein in the current condition.
source: Unfortunately, we could not locate the density of EA, indicating EA was not bound on the protein, probably due to reduced affinity of EA toward purified TRPC5 protein in the current condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of EA density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The apo state hTRPC5 structure closely resembles previously published apo mouse TRPC5 structure (PDB ID: 6AEI) with RMSD of 1.844 Å.
source: Therefore, we refer this structure as the 'apo' state of hTRPC5, which closely resembles previously published 'apo' mouse TRPC5 structure (PDB ID: 6AEI) (Duan et al., 2019) with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.844 Å.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and RMSD calculation.

claim: The overall architecture of inhibitor-bound hTRPC5 occupies 100 Å × 100 Å × 130 Å in three-dimensional space.
source: The overall architecture of inhibitor-bound hTRPC5 is similar to apo state, occupying 100 Å ×100 Å × 130 Å in three-dimensional (3D) space (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The hTRPC5 channel has a fourfold symmetric architecture with two-layer structure composed of the intracellular cytosolic domain layer and the transmembrane domain layer.
source: The fourfold symmetric channel has two-layer architecture, composed of the intracellular cytosolic domain (ICD) layer and the transmembrane domain (TMD) layer (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: F414 forms a π-π stacking interaction with the chlorophenyl ring of CMZ.
source: Among them, F414 forms a π-π stacking interaction with the chlorophenyl ring of CMZ.
evidence: This interaction is observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Side chains of Y374, M442, Y446, and P659 show hydrophobic interactions with CMZ.
source: Side chains of Y374, M442, Y446, and P659 show hydrophobic interactions with CMZ.
evidence: These interactions are observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Residues surrounding the CMZ-binding site are highly conserved between TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: Residues surrounding the CMZ-binding site are highly conserved between TRPC4 and TRPC5, in agreement with their similar selectivity for CMZ type inhibitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: F414M and S495A mutations did not change the potency of CMZ much.
source: We found mutations of F414M and S495A did not change the potency of CMZ much (Figure 2E, Table 2), while N443L decrease the potency (Figure 2E, Table 2), suggesting N443 is one of the structural determinants of TRPC subtype selectivity for CMZ inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2E and Table 2.

claim: N443L mutation decreases the potency of CMZ.
source: We found mutations of F414M and S495A did not change the potency of CMZ much (Figure 2E, Table 2), while N443L decrease the potency (Figure 2E, Table 2), suggesting N443 is one of the structural determinants of TRPC subtype selectivity for CMZ inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2E and Table 2.

claim: N443 is one of the structural determinants of TRPC subtype selectivity for CMZ inhibition.
source: We found mutations of F414M and S495A did not change the potency of CMZ much (Figure 2E, Table 2), while N443L decrease the potency (Figure 2E, Table 2), suggesting N443 is one of the structural determinants of TRPC subtype selectivity for CMZ inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing N443L decreases CMZ potency.

claim: F576 on pore helix forms π-π stacking interaction with the methylxanthine core of HC-070.
source: The side chain of F576 on pore helix forms π-π stacking interaction with the methylxanthine core of HC-070.
evidence: This interaction is observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: R557, Q573, and W577 form polar contacts with the hydroxypropyl tail of HC-070.
source: R557 on the loop linking S5 and pore helix (linker), Q573 and W577 on pore helix form polar contacts with the hydroxypropyl tail of HC-070.
evidence: These interactions are observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: F599, A602, and T603 on S6 from the adjacent subunit stabilize the hydroxypropyl tail of HC-070.
source: F599, A602, and T603 on S6 from the adjacent subunit also stabilize the hydroxypropyl tail.
evidence: These interactions are observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: F569 and L572 interact hydrophobically with the chlorophenyl ring of HC-070.
source: F569 and L572 interact hydrophobically with the chlorophenyl ring of HC-070 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: These interactions are observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Residues involved in HC-070 binding are absolutely conserved between hTRPC4 and hTRPC5 but not in TRPC3/6/7.
source: Residues involved in HC-070 binding are absolutely conserved between hTRPC4 and hTRPC5 but not in TRPC3/6/7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in agreement with the fact that HC-070 selectively inhibits TRPC4/5 with high potency compared with TRPC3/6/7 (Just et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation to Just et al., 2018.

claim: C525A mutation does not change the potency of HC-070 much.
source: We found that C525A does not change the potency of HC-070 much (Figure 3E, Table 3), while R557A, F569A, L572A, Q573A, F599A, and T603A show decreased potency (Figure 3E–F, Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3E and Table 3.

claim: R557A, F569A, L572A, Q573A, F599A, and T603A mutations show decreased potency for HC-070.
source: We found that C525A does not change the potency of HC-070 much (Figure 3E, Table 3), while R557A, F569A, L572A, Q573A, F599A, and T603A show decreased potency (Figure 3E–F, Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3E-F and Table 3.

claim: Q573A mutation dramatically decreased HC-070 potency, emphasizing the essential role of the hydrogen bond between Q573 and hydroxypropyl group of HC-070.
source: Notably, Q573A dramatically decreased HC-070 potency (Figure 3F, Table 3), emphasizing the essential role of the hydrogen bond between Q573 and hydroxypropyl group of HC-070.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3F and Table 3.

claim: F599N mutation increased the IC50 more dramatically than F599A mutation.
source: We also mutated F599 of hTRPC5 into the Asn (N in TRPC3/6) and found that F599N increased the IC50 more dramatically than F599A did, probably because F599N mutation perturbs the local hydrophobic environment of the HC-070-binding site and indirectly affects ligand binding (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The constriction of the ion conduction pore is formed by the side chains of I621, N625, and Q629, which represents the lower gate of hTRPC5.
source: Calculated pore profiles showed that the constriction is formed by the side chains of I621, N625, and Q629, which represents the lower gate of hTRPC5 (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is determined by pore radius calculation shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The smallest radius at the lower gate is below 1 Å, indicating the channel is in a nonconductive closed state.
source: The smallest radius at this gate is below 1 Å, indicating the channel is in a nonconductive closed state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is determined by pore radius calculation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A putative cation density inside VSLD, surrounded by E418, E421, N436, and D439, was observed in both CMZ and HC-070 maps.
source: A putative cation density inside VSLD, surrounded by E418 and E421 on S2 and N436, D439 on S3, was observed in both CMZ and HC-070 maps (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The E418Q-E421Q-D439N triple mutant channel cannot be activated by extracellular calcium.
source: We generate the E418Q-E421Q-D439N triple mutant (Duan et al., 2019) to abolish the cation-binding capability of this site and found the channel cannot be activated by extracellular calcium anymore (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting the essential role of this site for calcium activation.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cation-binding site in VSLD is essential for calcium activation of TRPC5.
source: We generate the E418Q-E421Q-D439N triple mutant (Duan et al., 2019) to abolish the cation-binding capability of this site and found the channel cannot be activated by extracellular calcium anymore (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting the essential role of this site for calcium activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing loss of calcium activation.

claim: CMZ can inhibit EA-elicited currents in the presence of 1 mM EGTA and 1 mM EDTA to chelate intracellular Ca2+.
source: We found that CMZ could inhibit EA-elicited currents in this condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting CMZ exerts its function independent of high intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CMZ exerts its function independent of high intracellular Ca2+.
source: We found that CMZ could inhibit EA-elicited currents in this condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting CMZ exerts its function independent of high intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology experiment showing CMZ inhibition in low calcium conditions.

claim: There is a zinc-binding site in the ankyrin repeat 4 (AR4)-linker helix (LH1) region coordinated by H178, C182, C184, and C187.
source: In ICD, there is another extra density found in the ankyrin repeat 4 (AR4)-linker helix (LH1) region (Figure 4D). The ion is coordinated by the side chains of H178 and C182 on the AR4-LH1 loop and C184 and C187 on the LH1 helix (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The zinc-binding site is likely an HC3-type zinc-binding site.
source: Based on the chemical environments for ion coordination, this is likely to be an HC3-type zinc-binding site, as observed previously in a bacteria glucokinase (Miyazono et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the coordination geometry and supported by citation to Miyazono et al., 2012.

claim: The residues coordinating the putative zinc ion are highly conserved in TRPC ion channels.
source: The residues coordinating the putative zinc ion are highly conserved in TRPC ion channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and mutation of C176A-C178A-C181A does not affect calcium activation or EA activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that this zinc-binding site might play other regulatory or structural roles, instead of ion channel gating.
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutation of C176A-C178A-C181A does not affect calcium activation or EA activation.
source: The residues coordinating the putative zinc ion are highly conserved in TRPC ion channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and mutation of C176A-C178A-C181A does not affect calcium activation or EA activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that this zinc-binding site might play other regulatory or structural roles, instead of ion channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The zinc-binding site might play regulatory or structural roles, instead of ion channel gating.
source: The residues coordinating the putative zinc ion are highly conserved in TRPC ion channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and mutation of C176A-C178A-C181A does not affect calcium activation or EA activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that this zinc-binding site might play other regulatory or structural roles, instead of ion channel gating.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of functional effect of mutations.

claim: A lipid molecule resembling diacylglycerol (DAG) was observed near the S5, pore helix, and S6 in the CMZ-bound hTRPC5 structure.
source: One lipid is located near the S5 and pore helix from one subunit and S6 from the adjacent subunit in the CMZ-bound hTRPC5. Its density highly resembles diacylglycerol (DAG) molecule which shows two acryl tails, but without phosphate group or headgroup of typical phospholipids (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: HPLC-MS experiments revealed that the purified protein sample contained markedly higher level of DAG compared to the purification buffer control.
source: In agreement with our structural observation, further HPLC-MS experiments revealed that the purified protein sample contained markedly higher level of DAG in comparison with the purification buffer control (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The free hydroxyl group of DAG forms polar contacts with Q573.
source: The free hydroxyl group of this DAG molecule forms polar contacts with Q573 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This interaction is observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The two hydrophobic tails of DAG interact with L528, Y524, F576, W577, V579, L617, V610, I611, and L616.
source: Its two hydrophobic tails interact with several hydrophobic residues: L528, Y524 on S5; F576, W577, and V579 on the pore helix; L617 on S6; and V610, I611, and L616 on S6 from adjacent subunit.
evidence: These interactions are observed in the high-resolution structure shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the HC-070-bound hTRPC5 map, the binding site of glycerol group of DAG was occupied by HC-070, while the binding site of two DAG tails was still filled by lipid-like densities.
source: Unexpectedly, in the map of HC-070-bound hTRPC5, we found that the binding site of glycerol group of DAG was occupied by HC-070, while the binding site of two DAG tails was still filled by lipid-like densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 7G), indicating the binding of the glycerol group of DAG and HC-070 are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7G.

claim: The binding of the glycerol group of DAG and HC-070 are mutually exclusive.
source: Unexpectedly, in the map of HC-070-bound hTRPC5, we found that the binding site of glycerol group of DAG was occupied by HC-070, while the binding site of two DAG tails was still filled by lipid-like densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 7G), indicating the binding of the glycerol group of DAG and HC-070 are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that HC-070 occupies the DAG glycerol binding site.

claim: The overall structures of hTRPC5 at different states are highly similar, with RMSD of 1.456 Å between CMZ-bound hTRPC5 and apo state.
source: The overall structures of hTRPC5 at different states are highly similar, with RMSD of 1.456 Å between CMZ-bound hTRPC5 and apo state; 0.926 Å between HC-070-bound hTRPC5 and apo state, although there is a little structural variation in details (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and RMSD calculation.

claim: The RMSD between HC-070-bound hTRPC5 and apo state is 0.926 Å.
source: The overall structures of hTRPC5 at different states are highly similar, with RMSD of 1.456 Å between CMZ-bound hTRPC5 and apo state; 0.926 Å between HC-070-bound hTRPC5 and apo state, although there is a little structural variation in details (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and RMSD calculation.

claim: The bottom of S3 segment and the S2-S3 linker in HC-070-bound structure have small conformational change compared to the apo hTRPC5.
source: In the TMD, the bottom of S3 segment and the S2-S3 linker in HC-070-bound structure have small conformational change compared to the apo hTRPC5 (Figure 5B), which may be due to the HC-070 binding.
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Inhibitors that bind IBP-A need to penetrate the plasma membrane first before reaching their binding site in VSLD.
source: IBP-A inside the VSLD is accessible from the intracellular side (Figure 6A). Inhibitors that bind IBP-A, such as CMZ and GFB-8438, need to penetrate the plasma membrane first before reaching their binding site in VSLD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural location of IBP-A shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CMZ, M084, and AC1903 are benzimidazole derivatives which can inhibit TRPC5 with IC50 values at 1.0–1.3, 8.2, and 14.7 μM, respectively.
source: CMZ, M084, and AC1903 are benzimidazole derivatives which can inhibit TRPC5 with IC50 values at 1.0–1.3, 8.2, and 14.7 μM, respectively (Richter et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Richter et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: CMZ, M084, and AC1903 probably share a common binding site at IBP-A due to their similar chemical structures.
source: Their similar chemical structures suggest that they probably share a common binding site at IBP-A (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity of these compounds shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: CMZ is 10- and 26-fold more potent against TRPC5 than TRPC3/6 and TRPC7, respectively.
source: CMZ is 10- and 26-fold more potent against TRPC5 than TRPC3/6 and TRPC7, respectively (Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richter et al., 2014.

claim: Both CMZ and GFB-8438 share a common set of interacting residues on hTRPC5 including L496, Y374, M442, N443, and R492.
source: Therefore, both CMZ and GFB-8438 share a common set of interacting residues on hTRPC5 including L496, Y374, M442, N443, and R492.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the binding sites of CMZ and GFB-8438.

claim: Structure-based hybridization of CMZ and GFB-8438 might exploit more interacting residues on hTRPC5 and thus enhance the inhibitor potency and selectivity.
source: More importantly, both CMZ and GFB-8438 have several nonoverlapping interacting residues on hTRPC5, suggesting that structure-based hybridization of CMZ and GFB-8438 might exploit more interacting residues on hTRPC5 and thus enhance the inhibitor potency and selectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the structural observations.

claim: Stabilization of VSLD in an inactive conformation might be a common scheme to inhibit TRP channel opening.
source: Based on the gating model of TRPV1, channel activation is associated with relative movements between VSLD and pore (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) and thus, stabilization of VSLD in an inactive conformation might be a common scheme to inhibit channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the gating model of TRPV1 and supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016.

claim: AM-1473, a potent antagonist of hTRPC6, binds at IBP-A in hTRPC6.
source: Indeed, AM-1473, a potent antagonist of hTRPC6, was found to bind at IBP-A in hTRPC6 as well (Bai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bai et al., 2020.

claim: IBP-A is the AMTB and TC-I 2014-binding sites in TRPM8.
source: Moreover, IBP-A is the AMTB and TC-I 2014-binding sites in TRPM8 (Diver et al., 2019), 2-APB-binding site in TRPV6 (Singh et al., 2018; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diver et al., 2019 and Singh et al., 2018.

claim: IBP-A is the 2-APB-binding site in TRPV6.
source: Moreover, IBP-A is the AMTB and TC-I 2014-binding sites in TRPM8 (Diver et al., 2019), 2-APB-binding site in TRPV6 (Singh et al., 2018; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2018.

claim: VSLD of TRP channels is a hotspot for drug discovery.
source: The studies suggest that VSLD of TRP channels is a hotspot for drug discovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple inhibitors bind at IBP-A in VSLD across different TRP channels.

claim: The DAG-binding pocket observed in hTRPC5 is structurally conserved in TRPC3/6 and is essential for TRPC3/6 channel activation by DAG and its analogues.
source: These data concertedly suggest that the DAG- binding pocket observed here in hTRPC5 is also structurally conserved in TRPC3/6 and is essential for TRPC3/6 channel activation by DAG and its analogues, such as OAG.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis studies in TRPC3/6 cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological compounds binding at IBP-B might affect TRPC channel gating either by acting on TRPC directly or by perturbing the normal function of DAG.
source: Pharmacological compounds binding at IBP-B might affect TRPC channel gating either by acting on TRPC directly or by perturbing the normal function of DAG.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that IBP-B overlaps with the DAG binding site.

claim: The binding of HC-070 at IBP-B replaces the glycerol group of DAG, stabilizes hTRPC5 in a closed state, and thus inhibits channel opening.
source: Here, we observed that the binding of HC-070 at this site replaces the glycerol group of DAG, stabilizes hTRPC5 in a closed state, and thus inhibits channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that HC-070 occupies the DAG glycerol binding site and the channel is in a closed state.

claim: The residues involved in HC-070 binding are absolutely identical between hTRPC5 and hTRPC4.
source: The residues involved in HC-070 binding are absolutely identical between hTRPC5 and hTRPC4, but they share only 20% similarities between TRPC4/5 and TRPC3/6/7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which explains the high selectivity of HC-070 for TRPC4/5 over TRPC3/6/7 (Just et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HC-070 shows inhibitory effect on heterotetrameric hTRPC1:C5 and hTRPC1:C4 with relatively lower potency compared to homotetrameric hTRPC4/5.
source: In addition, HC-070 shows inhibitory effect on heterotetrameric hTRPC1: C5 and hTRPC1: C4 with relatively lower potency compared to homotetrameric hTRPC4/5 (Just et al., 2018), probably because of the lower sequence identity between TRPC4/5 and TRPC1 (46% according to the sequence alignment) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Just et al., 2018 and sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pico145 is more potent against hTRPC4/5 than HC-070, possibly due to the substitution of chloride with trifluoromethoxy group on the chlorophenoxy ring.
source: It is reported that Pico145, an HC-070 analogue, is more potent against hTRPC4/5 than HC-070 (Just et al., 2018), possibly due to the substitution of chloride with trifluoromethoxy group on the chlorophenoxy ring of HC-070 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Just et al., 2018 and structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2G–H.

claim: Pico145 binds to hTRPC5 channel using a similar pose as HC-070, except the chlorophenoxy ring with a trifluoromethoxy group inserts into a cavity surrounded by L521, Y524, F576, and V610.
source: Indeed, recent structure study showed that Pico145 binds to hTRPC5 channel using a similar pose as HC-070, except the chlorophenoxy ring with a trifluoromethoxy group on it inserts into a cavity surrounded by L521, Y524, F576, and V610 of hTRPC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7J; Wright et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wright et al., 2020 and structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7J.

claim: AM237 is a TRPC5 activator with EC50 around 15–20 nM.
source: Another HC-070 analogue, AM237, is a TRPC5 activator with EC50 around 15–20 nM (Minard et al., 2019), and AM237 activates homomeric hTRPC5 channel instead of the heterotetrameric TRPC1: C5 channel (Minard et al., 2019), suggesting that AM237 also binds at IBP-B which is at the interface between adjacent subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minard et al., 2019.

claim: AM237 activates homomeric hTRPC5 channel instead of the heterotetrameric TRPC1:C5 channel.
source: Another HC-070 analogue, AM237, is a TRPC5 activator with EC50 around 15–20 nM (Minard et al., 2019), and AM237 activates homomeric hTRPC5 channel instead of the heterotetrameric TRPC1: C5 channel (Minard et al., 2019), suggesting that AM237 also binds at IBP-B which is at the interface between adjacent subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minard et al., 2019.

claim: AM237 binds at IBP-B which is at the interface between adjacent subunits.
source: Another HC-070 analogue, AM237, is a TRPC5 activator with EC50 around 15–20 nM (Minard et al., 2019), and AM237 activates homomeric hTRPC5 channel instead of the heterotetrameric TRPC1: C5 channel (Minard et al., 2019), suggesting that AM237 also binds at IBP-B which is at the interface between adjacent subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the selectivity of AM237 for homomeric channels.

claim: AM237 might activate hTRPC5 by pushing L521 on S5 using its chloride-phenoxy group.
source: Compared with Pico145, AM237 has an additional chloride atom on the phenoxy ring (Figure 6—figure supplement 2I), which makes the phenoxy group larger and this chloride atom might be in clash with L521 of hTRPC5. Therefore, AM237 might activate hTRPC5 by pushing L521 on S5 using its chloride-phenoxy group (Wright et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculated based on structural comparison and supported by citation to Wright et al., 2020.

claim: Mutations in IBP-B, including Q573T, F576A, and W577A, decrease the potency of AM237 on hTRPC5.
source: Consistent with our results of HC-070-binding site mutants, mutations in IBP-B, including Q573T, F576A, and W577A, decrease the potency of AM237 on hTRPC5 (Wright et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wright et al., 2020.

claim: An hTRPC6 agonist AM-0883 binds at IBP-B.
source: Recently, it is reported that an hTRPC6 agonist AM-0883 binds at IBP-B as well (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; Bai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bai et al., 2020.

claim: IBP-B is a common modulatory ligand-binding site in TRPC channels.
source: The identification of DAG lipid, TRPC inhibitor, and TRPC activator binding at IBP-B suggests that it is a common modulatory ligand-binding site in TRPC channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple ligands bind at IBP-B.

claim: BTDM, a high affinity inhibitor of hTRPC6, binds at IBP-C.
source: BTDM, a high affinity inhibitor of hTRPC6, binds at IBP-C (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Tang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2018.

claim: When BTDM is not supplied, IBP-C is occupied by a putative phospholipid.
source: When BTDM is not supplied, IBP-C is occupied by a putative phospholipid (Bai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bai et al., 2020.

claim: Mutations of G503/G504 to serine on S4-S5 linker in TRPC4/5 lead to constitutive activation of the channels.
source: In TRPC4/5, mutations of G503/G504 to serine on S4-S5 linker lead to constitutive activation of the channels (Beck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beck et al., 2013.

claim: Vanilloid agonist resiniferatoxin (RTX), vanilloid antagonist capsazepine, and an endogenous phosphatidylinositol bind at IBP-C on TRPV1.
source: In addition, vanilloid agonist resiniferatoxin (RTX), vanilloid antagonist capsazepine, and an endogenous phosphatidylinositol bind at IBP-C on TRPV1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016.

claim: IBP-C is important for the gating of both TRPC and TRPV channels.
source: These data together suggest that IBP-C is important for the gating of both TRPC and TRPV channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple ligands affecting channel gating bind at IBP-C.
